source.title: Curriculum-Guided Layer Scaling for Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Karanpartap Singh; Neil Band; Ehsan Adeli

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper does not fit or test scaling laws, but it reports paired perplexity and downstream results that qualify the version claiming downstream performance tracks pretraining loss: at the 2.5B-token setting, CGLS improves downstream average accuracy while worsening Pile perplexity relative to the randomized baseline.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. for a compute formula and uses the Chinchilla parameter-to-data ratio to set a 20B-token experiment, but does not test power-law loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its perplexity and downstream benchmark comparisons bear on V6 only. Other curriculum and layer-scaling comparisons are not scaling-law tests.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on curriculum-guided layer stacking. It borrows the Chinchilla 20× token/parameter ratio and Kaplan's 6ND FLOP formula as tools. It reports only its own method against compute-matched baselines. It fits no scaling relation and sweeps no scale. The perplexity-versus-downstream mismatch compares training recipes at a fixed size and budget. That is a related but different construct from V6's 'improves predictably with scale or with pretraining loss', so it is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a V6 test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that CGLS improves downstream performance under compute-matched training at both scales, at 20B tokens, and in code domain shift. They note that at 2.5B tokens the randomized baseline had better perplexity. They state this discrepancy disappears at 20B tokens, where CGLS improves both perplexity and accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates progressive layer expansion synchronized with data curricula; it does not use or fit the original scaling-law procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity and downstream performance differ by training recipe and token budget; the paper reports that at 2.5B tokens the randomized baseline has lower perplexity while CGLS performs better on reasoning tasks, whereas at 20B tokens CGLS improves both perplexity and downstream accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed size and compute (2.5B tokens), CGLS has worse Pile perplexity than the randomized baseline but higher downstream average at both 124M and 1.2B scales. Among the baselines, ordering is mixed: GPT-2 MIDAS has worse perplexity (30.70) but a higher average (35.56) than the randomized baseline. At 20B tokens the mismatch disappears.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across training recipes or inductive biases at a fixed model size and compute, lower held-out pretraining loss does not reliably imply higher downstream accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026), as stated in the text.
record.problems: The comparisons are not a systematic scaling-law sweep and do not fit predictive curves. The paired perplexity/downstream results are from selected recipes and budgets, and most table results have no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the other Table 1 and Table 3 method rows because the extracted rows already capture the paper's explicitly discussed mismatch at 2.5B tokens and the 20B-token comparison; these remaining method-level values do not add a distinct conclusion about loss-performance predictability.

untested.parts: No sweep or power-law fit over parameters, tokens or compute.
Chinchilla ratio is used as a setting, not tested.
Starting-depth ablations concern a progressive-growth schedule, not fixed-parameter shape effects on loss.
The code domain-shift run fits no scaling form.
There is no systematic scale sweep and no fit of downstream performance against scale or loss. There are only recipe comparisons at two sizes and two budgets.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Remaining Table 1 method rows (curricularized, layer-scaling-only, MIDAS): perplexity and average accuracy. These are needed to judge loss–downstream ordering across recipes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'challenges' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. The rows compare the study's own method with baselines and do not measure predictability with scale. Oddity: the randomized baseline's Pile perplexity is 26.33 at 20B tokens versus 20.83 at 2.5B tokens for the same ~1B model. This goes against loss falling with tokens, but the evaluation setups may differ and the paper does not comment, so it is not treated as V1 evidence. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or systematic sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
The 20× data/parameter ratio is cited and used for an experiment, but the paper does not find or test compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
The paper varies starting depth and layer-growth schedules, but does not test how depth or width affects held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
The code-pretraining experiment does not test whether power-law forms transfer to other regimes.

The paper compares held-out perplexity and downstream scores across selected training recipes and token budgets; it does not fit a predictive relationship or test downstream scaling across a systematic model-size sweep.
No scaling-law exponents or fitting choices are compared.

relation.reason: Scaling-law findings guide experimental budgets; the reported recipe comparisons do not establish or refute any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Section 4.2 uses the Chinchilla token/parameter ratio and a compute approximation to set method-comparison budgets. Results evaluate CGLS against baselines without fitting or testing a scaling law or downstream predictive relation.

source_check.notes: Token counts denote compute-budget scales: Section 4.2 explicitly defines 2.5B full-depth-equivalent tokens, with progressive methods processing more token updates. Accuracy values are percentages; the paper describes Llama-3.2-1B as both 1.2B and 1B parameters.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Compute-matched 2.5B-token comparisons of CGLS with the randomized baseline
reader_labels.reason: CGLS has higher average downstream accuracy but worse Pile perplexity at both model scales, so downstream performance does not consistently track pretraining loss in these comparisons (r1-r6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: At this setting, the lower Pile perplexity and higher downstream average move together, but the single recipe comparison does not establish a predictive scaling relationship (r7-r9).
